claim: Neoblasts are adult stem cells (ASCs) in planarians that sustain cell replacement during homeostasis and regeneration of any missing tissue.
source: Neoblasts are adult stem cells (ASCs) in planarians that sustain cell replacement during homeostasis and regeneration of any missing tissue.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about neoblasts supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The X1 population is >90% piwi-1+.
source: Studies have shown that the X1 population is >90% piwi-1+, and this gate has been used as the stem cell fraction in comparative transcriptomic studies (Reddien et al., 2005b; Eisenhoffer et al., 2008; Abril et al., 2010; Sandmann et al., 2011; Labbe et al., 2012; Onal et al., 2012; Resch et al., 2012; Solana et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies that characterized the X1 population.

claim: The X2 cell population is only 10–20% piwi-1+.
source: The X2 cell population is only 10–20% piwi-1+ and is thought to be enriched with immediate postmitotic progeny of neoblasts.
evidence: Stated as an established fact with supporting citations in the context.

claim: DESeq analysis identified 2839 X1 and 1512 X2 transcripts with a p-value ≤ 0.01.
source: This identified 2839 X1 and 1512 X2 transcripts with a p-value ≤ 0.01 (Figure 1A,B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Directly supported by the computational analysis performed in this study and shown in Figure 1.

claim: X1 and X2 cells shared the majority of their transcriptional profiles.
source: It is important to note that X1 and X2 cells shared the majority of their transcriptional profiles (Figure 1C), and bona fide progeny markers can be highly expressed in the X1 fraction, while bona fide stem cell markers can be highly expressed in the X2 fraction (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by the hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: 32 new markers distinguish two main epithelial progenitor populations.
source: We identified 32 new markers distinguishing two main epithelial progenitor populations and a planarian homolog to the MEX3 RNA-binding protein (Smed-mex3-1) as a key regulator of lineage progression.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by WISH and dFISH experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: mex3-1 was required for generating differentiated cells of multiple lineages.
source: mex3-1 was required for generating differentiated cells of multiple lineages, while restricting the size of the stem cell compartment.
evidence: Supported by RNAi experiments showing loss of multiple lineage markers after mex3-1 knockdown.

claim: mex3-1 restricts the size of the stem cell compartment.
source: mex3-1 was required for generating differentiated cells of multiple lineages, while restricting the size of the stem cell compartment.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification showing expansion of piwi-1+ cells after mex3-1 RNAi.

claim: prog-1 and prog-2 represent members of a larger gene family of unknown function expressed throughout the epithelial lineage.
source: In addition, prog-1 and prog-2 represent members of a larger gene family of unknown function, expressed throughout this epithelial lineage.
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis showing at least 24 distinct family members.

claim: Knockdown of mex3-1 completely abolishes regenerative ability.
source: Knockdown of mex3-1 completely abolishes regenerative ability and halts the production of prog-1/2+ and AGAT-1+ postmitotic progeny populations.
evidence: Demonstrated by regeneration assays and WISH analysis after mex3-1 RNAi.

claim: mex3-1 knockdown halts the production of prog-1/2+ and AGAT-1+ postmitotic progeny populations.
source: Knockdown of mex3-1 completely abolishes regenerative ability and halts the production of prog-1/2+ and AGAT-1+ postmitotic progeny populations.
evidence: Shown by WISH analysis demonstrating loss of these markers after mex3-1 RNAi.

claim: piwi-1+ stem cells concomitantly increase in number after mex3-1 knockdown.
source: piwi-1+ stem cells concomitantly increase in number, an increase that was observed in all three neoblast subclasses.
evidence: Quantified by counting piwi-1+ cells in cross sections and by subclass markers.

claim: The increase in piwi-1+ stem cells after mex3-1 knockdown was observed in all three neoblast subclasses.
source: piwi-1+ stem cells concomitantly increase in number, an increase that was observed in all three neoblast subclasses.
evidence: Demonstrated by quantification of sigma, zeta, and gamma neoblast markers shown in Figure 5D.

claim: mex3-1(RNAi) worms have impaired contribution to tissue turnover.
source: Finally, mex3-1(RNAi) worms have impaired contribution to tissue turnover, as evidenced by drastically reduced production of lineage-restricted neoblast descendants and diminished cell addition towards multiple tissue types, in addition to the epithelium.
evidence: Supported by EdU and BrdU labeling experiments showing reduced incorporation into differentiated tissues.

claim: mex3-1 functions to maintain asymmetry in stem cell lineage progression by promoting postmitotic fates and suppressing self-renewal.
source: These results suggest that mex3-1 functions to maintain asymmetry in stem cell lineage progression by promoting postmitotic fates and suppressing self-renewal.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the combined data showing loss of progeny and expansion of stem cells.

claim: The predicted proteins encoded by prog-1 and prog-2 do not have clear homology to genes in other animals.
source: Interestingly, the predicted proteins encoded by prog-1 and prog-2 do not have clear homology to genes in other animals, including the genomes of other sequenced flatworms (Echinococcus multilocularis, Schistosoma mansoni, Macrostomum lignano—www.macgenome.org) (Berriman et al., 2009; Zheng et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on BLAST searches against other genomes.

claim: The PROG family consists of at least 24 distinct members across multiple transcriptomes in S. mediterranea.
source: However, we observed that they had low similarity to each other and represented a family of at least 24 distinct members across multiple transcriptomes in S. mediterranea, 15 of which were represented in the top 100 X2-enriched gene set (Sandmann et al., 2011; Solana et al., 2012; Currie and Pearson, 2013; Vogg et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis across multiple transcriptome databases.

claim: The only motif detected in PROG family proteins was a signal sequence at the N-terminal end, suggesting that these proteins are secreted.
source: The only motif that could be detected was a signal sequence at the N-terminal end of the predicted proteins, suggesting that these proteins are secreted.
evidence: Based on protein domain prediction analysis using SMART software.

claim: 40/120 transcripts were either not detectable or not specific by WISH.
source: We observed that 40/120 transcripts were either not detectable or not specific, and the remaining 80/120 genes could be binned into one of four categories (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on WISH analysis of candidate genes.

claim: 13/120 genes showed most intense expression in the bi-lobed brain and nervous system.
source: One category (13/120) contained genes with the most intense expression in the bi-lobed brain and nervous system, with low levels of expression elsewhere in the body.
evidence: Based on WISH expression patterns.

claim: 18/120 genes exhibited a predominantly stem cell-like expression pattern.
source: A second group of genes (18/120) exhibited a predominantly stem cell-like expression pattern, with or without brain expression, which was confirmed by high expression in the X1 cell fraction (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Based on WISH patterns and RNAseq data showing X1 enrichment.

claim: 17/120 genes were expressed in a variety of distinct patterns including the gut, pharynx, peri-pharyngeal region, and neck.
source: A third subset of genes was expressed in a variety of distinct patterns including the gut, pharynx, peri-pharyngeal region, and neck (17/120) (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on WISH expression patterns.

claim: 32/120 genes exhibited an expression pattern highly similar to prog-1, prog-2, and AGAT-1.
source: Finally, the fourth and largest group (32/120) consisted of genes with an expression pattern highly similar to those of the known early and late progeny markers prog-1, prog-2, and AGAT-1, which are sub-epithelial across the entire animal with expression anterior to the photoreceptors (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) (Eisenhoffer et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on WISH expression patterns compared to known markers.

claim: 13/32 prog-like transcripts showed similar kinetics of down-regulation as prog-1 and prog-2, being almost completely lost by 48 hr post-irradiation.
source: We observed that 13/32 transcripts showed similar kinetics of down-regulation as the early progeny markers prog-1 and prog-2 and were almost completely lost by 48 hr post-irradiation (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on time-course WISH analysis after irradiation.

claim: 19/32 prog-like transcripts showed the majority of loss beyond 48 hr post-irradiation, consistent with being late progeny markers.
source: The remaining 19/32 transcripts showed the majority of loss beyond 48 hr post-irradiation, consistent with being late progeny markers (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on time-course WISH analysis after irradiation.

claim: All WThighXlow genes grouped as late progeny and were the only genes with detectable expression at 7 days post-irradiation.
source: Interestingly, all WThighXlow genes grouped as late progeny, and moreover, were the only genes with detectable expression at 7 days post-irradiation.
evidence: Based on irradiation time-course WISH analysis.

claim: 7.2% ± 2.1 of prog-1+ cells were piwi-1+.
source: Congruent with previous studies, we found a small amount of overlap between piwi-1 with prog-1, and minimal with AGAT-1: 7.2% ± 2.1 of prog-1+ cells were piwi-1+, while merely 0.29% ± 0.50 of AGAT-1+ cells were piwi-1+ (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on dFISH quantification experiments.

claim: 0.29% ± 0.50 of AGAT-1+ cells were piwi-1+.
source: Congruent with previous studies, we found a small amount of overlap between piwi-1 with prog-1, and minimal with AGAT-1: 7.2% ± 2.1 of prog-1+ cells were piwi-1+, while merely 0.29% ± 0.50 of AGAT-1+ cells were piwi-1+ (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on dFISH quantification experiments.

claim: Only 5.4% ± 2.4 of prog-1+ cells co-expressed low levels of AGAT-1.
source: In contrast to a previous study that found nearly 45% overlap between the progeny populations (Eisenhoffer et al., 2008), we found that only 5.4% ± 2.4 of prog-1+ cells co-expressed low levels of AGAT-1, while 5.2% ± 3.2 of AGAT-1+ cells had prog-1 expression.
evidence: Based on dFISH quantification experiments, contrasting with previous findings.

claim: 5.2% ± 3.2 of AGAT-1+ cells had prog-1 expression.
source: In contrast to a previous study that found nearly 45% overlap between the progeny populations (Eisenhoffer et al., 2008), we found that only 5.4% ± 2.4 of prog-1+ cells co-expressed low levels of AGAT-1, while 5.2% ± 3.2 of AGAT-1+ cells had prog-1 expression.
evidence: Based on dFISH quantification experiments.

claim: 17.8% ± 12.2 of prog-1+ cells were PIWI-1+.
source: In support of these data, we found that 17.8% ± 12.2 of prog-1+ cells to be PIWI-1+, while 1.6% ± 1.2 of AGAT-1+ cells had detectable PIWI-1 expression (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on dFISH with PIWI-1 immunolabeling.

claim: 1.6% ± 1.2 of AGAT-1+ cells had detectable PIWI-1 expression.
source: In support of these data, we found that 17.8% ± 12.2 of prog-1+ cells to be PIWI-1+, while 1.6% ± 1.2 of AGAT-1+ cells had detectable PIWI-1 expression (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on dFISH with PIWI-1 immunolabeling.

claim: Almost all newly identified late progeny transcripts examined exhibited substantial co-expression with AGAT-1, with overlap ranging from 100% with prog-1-7 to 55.5% with prog-1-4.
source: Almost all newly identified late progeny transcripts examined were found to exhibit substantial co-expression with AGAT-1, with overlap ranging from 100% with prog-1-7 to 55.5% with prog-1-4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Based on dFISH co-localization analysis.

claim: Every new epithelial progenitor marker assessed was down-regulated after zfp-1 RNAi.
source: We observed that every new epithelial progenitor marker assessed was down-regulated after zfp-1 RNAi, confirming that these genes were indeed expressed in epithelial progenitors (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on WISH analysis in zfp-1 RNAi animals.

claim: RNAi against prog-1 and prog-2 separately or together did not yield any detectable phenotype.
source: In agreement with previous data, RNAi against prog-1 and prog-2 separately or together did not yield any detectable phenotype (Eisenhoffer et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on RNAi screening experiments, consistent with previous findings.

claim: None of the new epithelial progenitor markers yielded phenotypes upon knockdown.
source: Unexpectedly, none of the new epithelial progenitor markers yielded phenotypes upon knockdown either, suggestive of considerable functional redundancy among these genes.
evidence: Based on RNAi screening experiments.

claim: mex3-1(RNAi) was completely penetrant and lethal, resulting in ventral curling, head regression, and dorsal lesioning during homeostasis.
source: mex3-1(RNAi) was completely penetrant and lethal, resulting in ventral curling, head regression, and dorsal lesioning during homeostasis, as well as loss of regenerative ability after amputation (Figure 3A–C), indicative of epithelial homeostasis defects as well as overall stem cell impairment (Bardeen and Baetjer, 1904; Reddien et al., 2005a).
evidence: Based on phenotypic observations of mex3-1 RNAi animals.

claim: mex3-1(RNAi) animals lost regenerative ability after amputation.
source: mex3-1(RNAi) was completely penetrant and lethal, resulting in ventral curling, head regression, and dorsal lesioning during homeostasis, as well as loss of regenerative ability after amputation (Figure 3A–C), indicative of epithelial homeostasis defects as well as overall stem cell impairment (Bardeen and Baetjer, 1904; Reddien et al., 2005a).
evidence: Based on regeneration assays shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Two other MEX3 homologs in S. mediterranea (mex3-2 and mex3-3) were neither irradiation-sensitive nor produced observable phenotypes after knockdown.
source: Using reciprocal BLAST, we identified two other MEX3 homologs in S. mediterranea (mex3-2 and mex3-3, transcripts SmedASXL_000637 and SmedASXL_01505, respectively), which both contained two KH RNA-binding domains and had top reciprocal BLAST hits in mouse, fly, and C. elegans. These additional MEX3 homologs were neither irradiation-sensitive nor produced observable phenotypes after knockdown and thus not investigated further (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on RNAseq data and RNAi experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: mex3-1 showed >fivefold enrichment in the X2 fraction over irradiated worms but also exhibited significant expression in the X1 stem cell fraction.
source: By RNAseq, mex3-1 showed >fivefold enrichment in the X2 fraction over irradiated worms but also exhibited significant expression in the X1 stem cell fraction (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on RNAseq quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: mex3-1 was widely expressed in stem cells, early progeny, and late progeny.
source: Analysis of mex3-1 using dFISH with lineage markers confirmed that mex3-1 was widely expressed in stem cells, early progeny, and late progeny (Figure 3F).
evidence: Based on dFISH co-localization analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Knockdown of mex3-1 leads to a rapid decline of the two progeny populations but not of stem cells.
source: Knockdown of mex3-1 leads to a rapid decline of the two progeny populations but not of stem cells (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), with the majority of progeny gene expression lost by 6 days after RNAi (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on WISH time-course analysis shown in Figure 4A and supplements.

claim: The majority of progeny gene expression was lost by 6 days after mex3-1 RNAi.
source: Knockdown of mex3-1 leads to a rapid decline of the two progeny populations but not of stem cells (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), with the majority of progeny gene expression lost by 6 days after RNAi (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on detailed time-course WISH analysis.

claim: mex3-1(RNAi) animals had comparable levels of cell death to control worms up until 9 days after RNAi, but significantly higher levels from 12 days and onward.
source: Quantification of TUNEL showed that mex3-1(RNAi) animals had comparable levels of cell death to control worms up until 9 days after RNAi, but significantly higher levels from 12 days and onward (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on TUNEL quantification shown in Figure 4C.

claim: mex3-1(RNAi) worms showed significantly increased levels of proliferation at every time point examined.
source: We observed significantly increased levels of proliferation in mex3-1(RNAi) worms at every time point examined (Figure 4D), which suggested that stem cell division was not impeded by mex3-1 knockdown.
evidence: Based on H3P immunolabeling quantification shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Worms pulsed with F-ara-EdU at 6 or 9 days after mex3-1 RNAi and fixed 24 hr later showed significantly increased numbers of total EdU-labeled cells compared to controls.
source: Worms pulsed at either 6 or 9 days after RNAi and fixed 24 hr later showed significantly increased numbers of total EdU-labeled cells in mex3-1(RNAi) animals compared to controls (Figure 5A), demonstrating that during phenotypic progression, a greater number of cells were entering the cell cycle.
evidence: Based on EdU labeling experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: FACS profiles of mex3-1(RNAi) animals at day 9 revealed relatively normal proportions of cells in both the X1 and X2 gates.
source: FACS profiles of mex3-1(RNAi) animals at day 9 revealed relatively normal proportions of cells in both the X1 and X2 gates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), further evidence that stem cells were progressing through the cell cycle and not arrested at 4C DNA in the X1 gate.
evidence: Based on FACS analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Sublethally irradiated mex3-1(RNAi) worms expanded piwi-1+ stem cell numbers over time but produced disproportionately fewer prog-1+ progeny than control worms.
source: Sublethally irradiated mex3-1(RNAi) worms expanded piwi-1+ stem cell numbers over time but produced disproportionately fewer prog-1+ progeny than control worms (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on sublethal irradiation experiments and quantification shown in Figure 5B.

claim: By 6 days after mex3-1 RNAi, there were highly significant increases in the number of piwi-1+ stem cells compared to controls, which rose to a 50% increase by day 12.
source: By 6 days after RNAi, we observed highly significant increases in the number of piwi-1+ stem cells in mex3-1(RNAi) animals compared to controls, which rose to a 50% increase by day 12 (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on quantification of piwi-1+ cells in cross sections shown in Figure 5C.

claim: All three neoblast subclasses (zeta, sigma, gamma) were significantly increased by approximately 50% in mex3-1(RNAi) animals at 12 days after RNAi.
source: Assessment at 12 days after RNAi revealed that all three subclasses were significantly increased by approximately 50% in mex3-1(RNAi) animals compared to controls (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on quantification of subclass markers shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 7 days following EdU administration, numerous EdU+ cells were present in the epithelium of control(RNAi) worms, but virtually none had been incorporated into the epithelium in mex3-1(RNAi) animals.
source: 7 days following EdU administration, numerous EdU+ cells were present in the epithelium of control(RNAi) worms, but virtually none had been incorporated into the epithelium in mex3-1(RNAi) animals (Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on EdU chase experiments shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Following amputation, mex3-1(RNAi) worms failed to re-establish the expression of epithelial genes at wounding sites.
source: Additionally, following amputation, mex3-1(RNAi) worms failed to re-establish the expression of epithelial genes at wounding sites, demonstrating that during both homeostasis and regeneration, mex3-1 is required for specification and differentiation of epithelial cell types (van Wolfswinkel et al., 2014) (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on dFISH analysis of regenerating blastemas shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Quantification of lineage-restricted neoblast progeny in intact mex3-1(RNAi) worms 12 days after RNAi showed significant reductions in all examined cell types (chat, coe, ovo, FoxA, six1/2-2).
source: Quantification of lineage-restricted neoblast progeny in intact mex3-1(RNAi) worms 12 days after RNAi showed significant reductions in all examined cell types (Figure 6D).
evidence: Based on quantification of PIWI-1+ cells co-expressing lineage markers shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Virtually all chat+PIWI-1+ cells expressed mex3-1.
source: We observed that virtually all chat+PIWI-1+ cells expressed mex3-1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting a direct role for mex3-1 in regulating differentiation outside the epithelial lineage.
evidence: Based on triple-label dFISH shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: 5 days following labeling with BrdU, the entry of new cells into brain, intestine, and pharynx was significantly decreased in mex3-1(RNAi) animals.
source: Concordant with decreased production of lineage-restricted neoblast progeny, we also observed that 5 days following labeling with BrdU, the entry of new cells into brain, intestine, and pharynx was significantly decreased in mex3-1(RNAi) animals (Figure 6E, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on BrdU chase experiments shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Knockdown of p53 did not alter the numbers of PIWI-1+ovo+ eye- or PIWI-1+chat+ brain-specified neoblast progeny.
source: We found that knockdown of p53 did not alter the numbers of PIWI-1+ovo+ eye- or PIWI-1+chat+ brain-specified neoblast progeny (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), demonstrating a broader role for mex3-1 in differentiation.
evidence: Based on quantification in p53 RNAi animals shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: mex3-1 RNAi resulted in a significant increase in the number of piwi-1+PIWI-1+ cells and simultaneous decrease in piwi-1−PIWI-1+ cells compared to controls.
source: We found that mex3-1 RNAi resulted in a significant increase in the number of piwi-1+PIWI-1+ cells and simultaneous decrease in piwi-1−PIWI-1+ cells compared to controls (Figure 6F), supporting a general reduction in the ability of stem cells to progress to a postmitotic state.
evidence: Based on quantification of piwi-1 mRNA and PIWI-1 protein co-expression shown in Figure 6F.

claim: 13/59 known stem cell-specific transcripts were significantly upregulated upon knockdown of mex3-1 (p < 0.01).
source: In agreement with our data demonstrating hyper-proliferation and expansion of the entire stem cell compartment after mex3-1 knockdown, 13/59 known stem cell-specific transcripts were significantly upregulated upon knockdown of mex3-1 (p < 0.01, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Based on RNAseq analysis of mex3-1 RNAi animals shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: An approximately 1.5-fold increase in soxP-1, zfp-1, and piwi-1 transcripts was observed in mex3-1(RNAi) animals.
source: Importantly, we also observed an approximately 1.5-fold increase in soxP-1, zfp-1, and piwi-1 transcripts in mex3-1(RNAi) animals (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A; Supplementary file 4), concordant with the increase in stem cell subclasses quantified by cell counting (Figure 5C,D).
evidence: Based on RNAseq data, consistent with cell counting results.

claim: All but two of the new early and late progeny markers were severely down-regulated in the RNAseq data set for mex3-1(RNAi) animals compared to controls.
source: As anticipated from the effects of mex3-1(RNAi) on the loss of all epithelial progenitor markers by WISH analyses, all but two of our new early and late progeny markers were severely down-regulated in the RNAseq data set for mex3-1(RNAi) animals compared to controls (Figure 7A; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Based on RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The two transcripts that did not appreciably change after mex3-1 RNAi (sox9-1 and RPC-2) have very high X1 expression in addition to labeling epithelial progenitors.
source: The two transcripts that did not appreciably change (sox9-1 and RPC-2) have very high X1 expression in addition to labeling epithelial progenitors, which was not expected to change in mex3-1 RNAi.
evidence: Based on RNAseq data and expression patterns.

claim: 20/21 down-regulated and uncharacterized transcripts produced a prog-like pattern in control worms and exhibited severely reduced expression in mex3-1(RNAi) worms.
source: We found that 20/21 transcripts produced a prog-like pattern in control worms and exhibited severely reduced expression in mex3-1(RNAi) worms, as anticipated from RNAseq (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Based on WISH validation of RNAseq candidates shown in Figure 7B.

claim: SmedASXL_059179 was highly expressed near the proximal end of the pharynx, throughout the pharynx proper, and was similarly dependent on mex3-1 for its expression.
source: The remaining transcript, SmedASXL_059179, was highly expressed near the proximal end of the pharynx, throughout the pharynx proper, and was similarly dependent on mex3-1 for its expression (Figure 7B).
evidence: Based on WISH analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: PIWI-1+SmedASXL_059179+ cells were observed near the proximal base of the pharynx.
source: We predicted that SmedASXL_059179+ cells may represent a pharyngeal progenitor cell type, and indeed, we observed PIWI-1+SmedASXL_059179+ cells near the proximal base of the pharynx (Figure 7C).
evidence: Based on dFISH with PIWI-1 immunolabeling shown in Figure 7C.

claim: RNAi against SmedASXL_059179 did not result in apparent perturbations to pharynx function during homeostasis or regeneration.
source: However, no regulatory roles were uncovered for this gene, as RNAi against SmedASXL_059179 did not result in apparent perturbations to pharynx function during homeostasis or regeneration (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: Based on RNAi experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Epithelial progenitors are the predominant output of stem cells, most likely reflecting highest turnover needs as well as molecular complexity of this organ.
source: Combined with the revelation that zeta-neoblasts are the largest known lineage-restricted stem cell subclass in planarians, we conclude that epithelial progenitors are the predominant output of stem cells, most likely reflecting highest turnover needs as well as molecular complexity of this organ.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the preponderance of epithelial markers found in the X2 fraction and known biology.

claim: MEX3 is an RNA-binding translational repressor discovered in C. elegans with embryonic and post-embryonic developmental roles.
source: MEX3 is an RNA-binding translational repressor discovered in C. elegans with embryonic and post-embryonic developmental roles (Draper et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claim: MEX3 is a fundamental regulator of asymmetry in C. elegans, mediating one of the earliest steps of cell fate determination by restricting expression of the cell fate determinant pal-1 transcription factor to the posterior blastomere of the early embryo.
source: MEX3 is a fundamental regulator of asymmetry, mediating one of the earliest steps of cell fate determination in C. elegans by restricting expression of the cell fate determinant pal-1 transcription factor to the posterior blastomere of the early embryo (Draper et al., 1996; Huang et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claim: In adult C. elegans, MEX3 participates in the maintenance of germline stem cells (GSCs) by promoting proliferation, and is not required for GSCs to differentiate and undergo meiosis.
source: In adult C. elegans, MEX3 participates in the maintenance of germline stem cells (GSCs) by promoting proliferation, and interestingly, is not required for GSCs to differentiate and undergo meiosis (Ariz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claim: MEX3A overexpression increased levels of intestinal stem cell markers such as Bmi1 and Lgr5 in murine intestinal cell culture.
source: Recent work on MEX3A in murine intestinal cell culture showed that the master intestinal differentiation factor Cdx2, one of the vertebrate homologs of pal-1, is a target of MEX3A translational inhibition, and furthermore, MEX3A overexpression increased levels of intestinal stem cell markers such as Bmi1 and Lgr5 (Pereira et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from the literature.

claim: The findings in planarians combined with results in C. elegans and vertebrates suggest a conserved ancestral function for mex3 genes in cell fate choice.
source: Though the role of MEX3A in intestinal stem cell fate in vivo remains to be fully explored, these findings combined with our results in planarians suggest a conserved ancestral function for mex3 genes in cell fate choice.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparative analysis across species.

claim: Unlike zfp-1(RNAi) worms, mex3-1(RNAi) worms completely lose the ability to form any regenerative blastema.
source: Although both zfp-1 and mex3-1 are required for specification of epithelial-fated progeny, unlike zfp-1(RNAi) worms, mex3-1(RNAi) worms completely lose the ability to form any regenerative blastema.
evidence: Based on comparison of regeneration phenotypes between the two RNAi conditions.

claim: mex3-1 acts to mediate stem cell lineage asymmetry in the general stem cell pool and regulate all postmitotic lineages.
source: mex3-1 was further needed to prevent the expansion of the stem cell compartment, including sigma-, gamma-, and zeta-class neoblasts, which suggests that mex3-1 acts to mediate stem cell lineage asymmetry in the general stem cell pool and regulate all postmitotic lineages.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the broad effects observed across all neoblast subclasses.

claim: Both C. elegans and vertebrate MEX3 proteins have been shown to be translational repressors.
source: As both C. elegans and vertebrate MEX3 proteins have been shown to be translational repressors, it is likely that this molecular function has been conserved in planarians.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from the literature.

claim: mex3-1 acts as a repressor of stem cell identity and self-renewal genes in postmitotic progenitors to promote differentiation.
source: Thus, we propose a model of stem cell lineage progression with mex3-1 acting as a repressor of stem cell identity and self-renewal genes in postmitotic progenitors to promote differentiation (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the data and known MEX3 function.

claim: No planarian homolog to the conserved MEX3 target Cdx2/pal-1 could be found in existing transcriptomes or genomic sequence.
source: No planarian homolog to the conserved MEX3 target Cdx2/pal-1 could be found in existing transcriptomes or genomic sequence (Sánchez Alvarado et al., 2003; Robb et al., 2008; Abril et al., 2010; Sandmann et al., 2011; Labbe et al., 2012; Onal et al., 2012; Resch et al., 2012; Solana et al., 2012; Fernandes et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on BLAST searches against planarian sequence databases.

claim: Transcriptional analysis of mex3-1(RNAi) animals may be a promising avenue to discover rare and novel progeny markers.
source: With the evidence described in this study implicating mex3-1 as a regulator of multiple neoblast progeny for other tissues, transcriptional analysis of mex3-1(RNAi) animals may be a promising avenue to discover rare and novel progeny markers.
evidence: This is a proposed future direction based on the utility demonstrated in this study.

claim: The identification of SmedASXL_059179 as a pharyngeal marker with expression in PIWI-1+ cells demonstrates that lineage-restricted progeny are present outside the X1 and X2 gates.
source: The identification of one of these transcripts as a pharyngeal marker with expression in PIWI-1+ cells demonstrates that lineage-restricted progeny are present outside the X1 and X2 gates and merits the investment of future efforts toward screening further WThighXlow genes that are regulated by mex3-1 in order to uncover novel progenitors.
evidence: Based on the characterization of SmedASXL_059179 shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Smed-mex3-1 mediates asymmetric cell fate in planarian stem cell lineages, similar to MEX3's role in C. elegans embryogenesis.
source: Due to the well-known function of MEX3 in mediating asymmetric cell fates during Caenorhabditis elegans embryogenesis (Draper et al., 1996), we propose that Smed-mex3-1 mediates a similar process in planarian stem cell lineages.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on functional conservation across species.
